unit_evidence.original_text: On the morning of his seventh birthday the boy wakes before the city does. He lies still while it catches up to him — a shutter going up, a dog with an opinion, the first feet of the day on the stair street. He has a loose tooth. He works it with his tongue, saving it.

unit_evidence.original_text: From the kitchen, his mother beating eggs with a fork — the mixer frightens the batter, she says, and not today of all days. Lemon. There will be lemon under her nails until evening, and a fresh burn across her wrist, the old scar renewed annually.

unit_evidence.original_text: His father stands on a chair with a nail between his lips. The banner hangs crooked over the balcony door. It will hang crooked at every party this room ever holds.

unit_evidence.original_text: The apartment sits three floors above the café that lends out its chairs for every wedding, funeral and birthday on the hill. The stair street has a hundred and twelve steps, a dry fountain at the fortieth, laundry crossing overhead like signal flags. At the top a transformer hums one low note the neighborhood has agreed not to hear. From the balcony the boy can see the far hill with its cranes, building the same building since before he was born. Under everything, the water — a river or a sea, depending on which way the wind is working. Behind the flat, where the stair street gives out, is the hill nobody in this room has ever had a reason to climb. The morning smells of frying from the café, bleach from the stairwell, drains breathing after last night's rain.

unit_evidence.original_text: The guests come up the hundred and twelve steps and arrive breathing hard. The best friend is first, socks slipped down into his shoes, holding a plastic whistle he has already decided not to give away and will forget on the windowsill by dark. The girl with the braid goes straight for the cake to eat the sugar flowers off its shoulders, and is allowed to. The neighbor brings a dish nobody asked for, heavy, still hot through the towel, that everyone will finish. The twins arrive in matching shirts and spend the afternoon denying it. The uncles take the balcony and smoke, tapping ash into a flowerpot where nothing has ever grown.

unit_evidence.original_text: The cake comes out wearing seven candles. The room sings his name, stretching it to fit the tune, and somewhere inside the singing the tooth comes free; he holds it in his cheek. He decides he counted wrong. With the first slice he swallows a little blood along with the lemon, and tells no one.

unit_evidence.original_text: They play the game with the chairs. One chair is taken away. The music plays and they orbit the table, chair legs shrieking on the tile. The music stops. The neighbor's husband loses the first round, laughing, takes his glass out with him, and salutes the cranes.

unit_evidence.original_text: There is a year of the game when the music stops and he and a woman reach the same chair at the same instant, her hip hard against his hip. He loses on purpose. He carries his chair out to the balcony with his blood loud, and her laugh follows him out. Later she comes out for the cool, the singing behind her, and the balcony holds them the way it holds the chairs. Her mouth tastes of lemon and somebody's cigarette. His hands learn her between two verses — the notch of a hip, the damp heat under a waistband, a breast heavy in his palm through cotton. Her laugh goes quiet against his throat and stays. The empty chairs face the city. They put themselves right before the song needs her. After that it is she who begins the song, half a beat early, every year. Some years later her chair joins the rows. He does not watch that round.

unit_evidence.original_text: The stair street gets a rail bolted up its middle, then a chair that rides the rail. The fountain at the fortieth comes back to life one spring and runs water marked non-potable in three languages. The laundry moves indoors; the lines stay up, carrying nothing. The café changes hands and keeps its chairs. A boy still carries them up — a different boy every decade, the same complaint at the fortieth step. The transformer is swapped one winter for something silent, and the hill sleeps badly for months, missing a note nobody will admit to knowing. Across the water a second bridge goes up, lit at night like a pulse. Deliveries stitch the evening with the sound of patient insects.

unit_evidence.original_text: He keeps a flat the way other men keep a razor. One room over the funicular's middle station — a bed, a fork, a bicycle with good brakes. He has timed his exits. Any room in the city, under a minute, nothing left behind but heat in the sheets.

unit_evidence.original_text: Nights he works the middle station. Two cars run on one cable, the up car balanced against the down car; they meet at the loop outside his window, twelve seconds of lit glass level with lit glass, then apart. He checks tickets. He frees a jammed door with the flat of his hand. He passes a cellist her case through the gap and her fingers are all callus and no ring. The hill's bodies ride through him all night — clerks asleep standing up, boys wet from the pools, a man who rides down every midnight and is never on the up car.

unit_evidence.original_text: In March a woman with cold hands spends three nights with him. She walks her thumb down his spine one bone at a time and stops at the seventh. She presses once. Their father's plot: the bean rows gone over, the rain barrel low, the oil drum he burned his prunings in standing where it has always stood. They burn the drives one at a time. The stickers curl first. The heat comes off the drum in a wall and they stand closer than is comfortable, and the daughter keeps turning her face away and turning it back. The smell is wrong for a garden fire — plastic, and under the plastic something sweeter — and the drum spits, and her elder brother feeds it steadily, like a man paying a debt in installments. Two plots down an old man waters by flashlight and does not look over. His granddaughter sits beside his shortwave radio. He says he is listening for people on other planets. When a voice comes through, she carries the radio over. He listens, then shakes his head. She leaves it on the ground and goes home. On the hill above them the smoke shows against the last of the light.

pieces.title: Visiting Hours

unit_evidence.text: Visiting Hours

unit_evidence.original_text: The funicular's last stop is called the last stop. The hill continues without it. The steps begin at a rusted gate, propped open longer than anyone has been alive to prop it. They have been counted many times and never twice to the same number. She starts up in the early cool with the return half of her ticket in her pocket and water in a bottle and no reason she has said aloud. The steps are stone, then older stone, then stone that has given up being anything but hill. A rope rail runs beside them, polished to glass where hands have needed it, slack where they have not. In a niche the size of a loaf, wax stands on old wax, still warm at the wick, though she has met no one coming down. Her phone loses the city at the treeline and stays lost, a stone that used to sing. She puts it away. After the treeline the sounds peel away in the order they were added — the deliveries first, then the traffic, then the harbor bell, then the channel's whole patient business — until the loudest thing on the path is her own blood. The air changes hands somewhere in the last hundred steps. At the top the wall is low and white, mended in every mortar fashion there has ever been, and the gate stands open.

On the step sits a narrow gray cat, unhurried, one ear notched by something settled long ago. The cat considers her, decides she is expected, and says so. On a stand by the door lies the visitors' book, open, unattended, the hands in it drying centuries apart and the ink all one age. She does not sign yet. She has been up nine minutes. She has stopped checking the time.

unit_evidence.original_text: There are others. A woman in mourning, three hundred years out of fashion, lights her wax from the standing wax, exact, practiced. A child asks her, in a dialect the city has stopped losing sleep over, whether the boats still go out in pairs; she says yes, and the child is satisfied, and that is the whole transaction. Two men stand at the wall looking down at the city, each between his wars, and one of the wars has not happened yet. A goat looks at her over the wall and asks if the mule track has reopened; she says there is a funicular now; the goat withdraws, unconvinced.

The state funds them, he says — continuity of heritage; the debit goes out monthly, they are told. The box is separate. "The box is not for us. It lets you feel you've given something to a place that needs nothing." She puts a coin in anyway. "Everyone does," he says. "That is the feeling working." She asks how old the house is. Two thousand years, he says, or three; they are open toward both ends, and the paperwork is older than paper. In a side room a man who says he has no faith is asleep on a prayer mat. Someone has covered his feet.

Among the morning's coins lies one she knows the way she knows her own handwriting, worn smooth, older than the country. She closes the lid.

unit_evidence.original_text: The smuggler comes up at dusk, still drying, salt in his seams, a stain at his side that has stopped mattering. The book does not offer him a line. They struck him from the register at the water, he tells her, before the other thing. The crossing will never have him now, in any words. So he came up. He looks at her the way the shot look at the standing. "I had to exist to see it. It never had to see me." He stops, and starts again. "That's not — I had to be there. It didn't." She has nothing. She unscrews the cap and holds the bottle out. The cat, from the step, without opening her eyes: "The hill watched the city arrive. It is prepared to watch it leave."

İki el ötede oğlunun yüzü bir yabancının başparmağının altına giriyor. Kaşını bölen soluk çentik. Bir omuzları kalkık imza atıyorlar; tükenmez kalemlerin zinciri kısa. unit_evidence.original_text: Ziyaret Saatleri

unit_evidence.original_text: Fünikülerin son durağına son durak denir. Tepe onsuz devam eder. Basamaklar paslı bir kapıdan başlıyor. Kapı bugün yaşayan herkesten daha uzun zamandır açık duruyor. Basamaklar defalarca sayılmış; iki kez aynı sayı çıkmamış. Kadın sabahın serinliğinde tırmanmaya başlıyor. Cebinde biletinin dönüş yarısı, şişesinde su var; buraya neden geldiğiniyse yüksek sesle söylemiş değil. Önce taş basamaklardan geçiyor, sonra daha eski taşlardan, sonra da tepeden başka bir şey olmaktan vazgeçmiş taşlardan. Basamaklar boyunca bir halat korkuluk uzanıyor; ellerin tutunmaya ihtiyaç duyduğu yerleri cam gibi parlamış, duymadığı yerleri gevşek kalmış. Bir somun büyüklüğündeki nişte eski balmumunun üstüne balmumu yığılmış; fitilin dibinde hala sıcak. Oysa aşağı inen kimseyle karşılaşmadı. Telefonu ağaç sınırında şehri kaybedip öylece kalıyor: eskiden şarkı söyleyen bir taş. Telefonunu yerine kaldırıyor. Ağaç sınırından sonra sesler eklendikleri sırayla bir bir sıyrılıp gidiyor — önce teslimatların sesi, sonra trafik, sonra liman çanı, sonra kanalın sabırla sürüp giden bütün işi — sonunda patikadaki en yüksek ses kendi kanının sesi kalıyor. Hava son yüz basamağın bir yerinde el değiştiriyor. Tepedeki alçak, beyaz duvarı gelmiş geçmiş her harç usulüyle onarmışlar; kapı açık duruyor.

unit_evidence.original_text: Küçük manastır badana beyazı ve is karası. Avlusu bir yelken büyüklüğünde, odaları kağıt dokusu alana dek süpürülmüş. Basamakta ince, gri bir kedi telaşsızca oturuyor. Bir kulağındaki çentik çok eskiden kapanmış bir meselenin izi. Kedi onu tartıyor, beklendiğine karar veriyor ve bunu söylüyor. Kapının yanındaki sehpada ziyaretçi defteri açık duruyor; başında kimse yok. İçindeki el yazıları yüzyıllar arayla kuruyor, ama bütün mürekkep aynı yaşta. Henüz imzalamıyor. Dokuz dakikadır yukarıda. Saate bakmayı bıraktı.
